video.title: Why Your Forehand Sprays, and How to Fix It

classification.reason: The coach gives executable drills including hitting with an open palm to innervate the top haptic reference and testing face control with self-drop feeds.

problem.title_as_question: Why Does Your Forehand Spray, and How Can You Fix It?
problem.definition: The player lacks racket face control and sprays shots because a broken haptic sensory link at the top of the handle prevents the brain from perceiving momentum and calibrating contact.
problem.target_player: Players with decent biomechanics whose forehand sprays due to poor racket face feel or handle fit

symptoms.description: The player sprays the ball and lacks consistent racket face control in the hitting zone.
The player cannot feel the pressure profile or whether the racket is loading and releasing properly.
The player struggles to smoothly feed balls out of hand using their forehand grip compared to continental.

causes.statement: An oversized handle breaks the sensory link so the brain cannot perceive racket momentum during loading and contact.
The handle gets jammed against the fingers rather than allowing hand contours to sit flush and caress the bevels.
The top face of the handle is too wide, creating an air gap that disconnects the top haptic reference point.
Missing the top pressure reference leaves the player unable to feel where the load builds and releases.

angles.summary: High-fidelity haptic feedback from both the bottom fingers and top flush palm allows instant auto-correction of timing and face angle.
The coach deliberately creates a gap at the top contact point to demonstrate how instantly face control and targeting deteriorate.
Using Alcaraz's grip structure naturally causes the swing to self-organize into a bigger loop to feel the racket momentum.
Continental grip feels effortless for hand feeding because the V of the hand sits fully flush against the narrow bevel, providing complete face awareness.

solutions.summary: Check whether the handle size or top face is too wide by verifying that hand contours sit flush rather than crashing into the fingers, switching to a thinner grip if needed.
Nestle the narrow edge of the handle fully into the V of the hand and hit balls with an open palm to isolate and feel the racket's momentum through that single reference.
solutions.external_goal: Drive the ball onto the red target

solutions.summary: Accumulate roughly a thousand open-palm swings over a month to force the brain to fully innervate the top handle reference and internalize the hitting slot.
Test racket face innervation by attempting to accurately self-drop and feed balls out of hand using your forehand grip.
solutions.external_goal: Feed the ball out of your hand accurately

solutions.summary: Once you can successfully rally with an open hand, place the bottom fingers back onto the handle while maintaining the identical momentum pattern.
solutions.external_goal: Maintain rally control with the full hand replaced
